title: Paul in Corinth
overview: Acts 18 details the Apostle Paul's ministry in Corinth, a pivotal city in his missionary journeys. After leaving Athens, Paul meets Aquila and Priscilla, fellow tentmakers, with whom he partners in both work and ministry. He boldly preaches in the synagogue, faces opposition, and receives divine encouragement to continue. The chapter highlights the conversion of Crispus, the synagogue ruler, and the protection Paul experiences under Gallio, the Roman proconsul. Paul’s departure to Ephesus and subsequent ministry there introduces Apollos, an eloquent teacher who is further instructed by Aquila and Priscilla. This chapter showcases the expansion of the early church through teaching, perseverance amid opposition, and the importance of mentorship in Christian growth.
structure:
**Verses 1-11: Paul’s Ministry in Corinth.** Paul arrives in Corinth, partners with Aquila and Priscilla, preaches in the synagogue, and witnesses conversions including Crispus. God encourages Paul through a vision to boldly continue his work.

**Verses 12-17: Opposition and Legal Protection.** The Jewish leaders bring Paul before Gallio accusing him of violating the law, but Gallio dismisses the case, allowing Paul to continue unhindered.

**Verses 18-23: Paul’s Departure and Strengthening the Churches.** Paul leaves Corinth, travels to Ephesus where he briefly ministers, then returns to Antioch after greeting the church in Caesarea. He strengthens disciples in Galatia and Phrygia.

**Verses 24-28: Apollos’ Ministry in Ephesus.** Apollos, an eloquent and knowledgeable teacher, arrives in Ephesus. Aquila and Priscilla instruct him more fully in the gospel, and he later ministers effectively in Achaia.

keyVerses.text: Then spake the Lord to Paul in the night by a vision, Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace:
keyVerses.significance: This verse reveals God's direct encouragement to Paul, affirming divine presence and calling him to boldness despite opposition. It underscores the theme of divine guidance in the missionary task.

keyVerses.text: And when they opposed themselves, and blasphemed, he shook his raiment, and said unto them, Your blood be upon your own heads; I am clean: from henceforth I will go unto the Gentiles.
keyVerses.significance: Paul’s decisive break from persistent Jewish opposition marks a pivotal moment in the mission to the Gentiles, emphasizing the gospel’s expanding reach beyond Israel.

keyVerses.text: And when Paul was now about to open his mouth, Gallio said unto the Jews, If it were a matter of wrong or wicked lewdness, O ye Jews, reason would that I should bear with you: But if it be a question of words and names, and of your law, look ye to it; for I will be no judge of such matters.
keyVerses.significance: Gallio’s refusal to judge religious disputes provides Paul legal protection, illustrating God’s providential care in advancing the gospel despite opposition.

keyVerses.text: For he mightily convinced the Jews, and that publickly, shewing by the scriptures that Jesus was Christ.
keyVerses.significance: This verse highlights Apollos’ powerful scriptural teaching, affirming the centrality of Christ as Messiah and the importance of sound doctrine in evangelism.

characters.name: Paul
characters.description: The apostle and missionary who preaches boldly in Corinth, partners with Aquila and Priscilla, faces opposition, receives divine encouragement, and continues his mission to strengthen churches.

characters.name: Aquila and Priscilla
characters.description: Jewish tentmakers who recently left Rome, they host Paul, assist in ministry, and later instruct Apollos more perfectly in the way of God, exemplifying Christian partnership and discipleship.

characters.name: Gallio
characters.description: Roman proconsul of Achaia who dismisses the Jewish accusations against Paul, providing legal protection that allows the gospel to flourish unhindered in Corinth.

characters.name: Apollos
characters.description: An eloquent and knowledgeable Jew from Alexandria who, after being instructed by Aquila and Priscilla, becomes a powerful preacher of Christ in Ephesus and Achaia.

characters.name: Crispus
characters.description: Chief ruler of the Corinthian synagogue who believes in Jesus along with his household, marking a significant conversion among Jewish leadership in the city.

themes.description: God’s direct communication to Paul in a vision encourages boldness and perseverance, demonstrating divine involvement in the spread of the gospel.
Paul’s decision to focus on Gentiles after Jewish opposition highlights the gospel’s universal scope and God’s plan to include all nations.
The collaboration between Paul, Aquila, Priscilla, and Apollos illustrates the importance of mutual support and teaching within the early church.
Gallio’s refusal to prosecute Paul shows God’s providential protection over His servants, allowing the gospel to advance despite opposition.
Apollos’ use of the Scriptures to prove Jesus as the Christ emphasizes the foundational role of God’s Word in evangelism and teaching.

historicalContext: This chapter is set in the mid-first century AD during Paul’s second missionary journey, approximately AD 50-52. Corinth was a major Roman city in Achaia, known for its commerce, diverse population, and moral challenges. The expulsion of Jews from Rome by Emperor Claudius (c. AD 49) led Aquila and Priscilla to relocate to Corinth, where they met Paul. Roman political structures, such as the proconsulship of Gallio, played a role in the legal environment, affecting how religious disputes were handled. The synagogue was a central place for Jewish teaching and debate, and the early Christian mission often began there.

theologicalInterpretations.description: Reformed theology emphasizes God’s sovereign providence in protecting Paul and advancing the gospel. The vision in verses 9-10 is seen as assurance of God’s covenant faithfulness to His promises.
Dispensationalists highlight the shift in Paul’s ministry focus from Jews to Gentiles in verse 6 as a key moment in God’s unfolding plan for the church age distinct from Israel.
Early church interpreters like Chrysostom focus on the example of Aquila and Priscilla as models of Christian hospitality and teaching, and on Paul’s boldness as an example for all believers.

crossReferences.connection: Paul greets Aquila and Priscilla, showing their ongoing partnership in ministry.
Paul mentions baptizing Crispus, connecting to his conversion in Acts 18.
Jesus’ teaching about the harvest parallels Paul’s mission to reach the many people in Corinth.
Paul’s emphasis on sound teaching and warning against false doctrines relates to Apollos’ instruction by Aquila and Priscilla.
The call to remember those in prison and suffering echoes the trials Paul faced during his ministry.

application: Trust God’s guidance and encouragement when facing opposition in ministry or daily life.
Engage in faithful partnership and discipleship within the church community to strengthen one another.
Be bold in proclaiming the gospel, even when rejected by some.
Rely on Scripture as the authoritative foundation for teaching and defending the faith.
Recognize God’s providential protection over His servants and remain steadfast in mission.
Welcome and instruct new believers and teachers to grow in the knowledge of Christ.
conclusion: Acts 18 powerfully illustrates the dynamic expansion of the early church through faithful proclamation, divine encouragement, and strategic partnerships. Paul’s ministry in Corinth, supported by Aquila and Priscilla, demonstrates how God’s providence protects and advances the gospel amid opposition. The chapter’s emphasis on Scripture, boldness, and discipleship continues to inspire believers to persevere in mission, nurture one another, and trust God’s sovereign hand in all circumstances.
timeline: c. AD 50-52 - Paul's Ministry in Corinth and Ephesus

definitions.definition: Craftsmen who made tents, a trade practiced by Paul, Aquila, and Priscilla to support themselves while ministering.
A Jewish place of worship and teaching where Paul frequently preached and reasoned with Jews and Gentiles.
A Roman official governing a province; Gallio was proconsul of Achaia, responsible for legal matters in Corinth.
To speak irreverently or disrespectfully about God or sacred things, an accusation faced by Paul.
The baptism preached by John the Baptist focusing on repentance, which Apollos knew before receiving fuller Christian teaching.

outline.heading: Opposition and Legal Proceedings
outline.description: Jewish leaders accuse Paul before Gallio, but the proconsul dismisses the case, protecting Paul and allowing the gospel to advance.

outline.heading: Paul’s Departure and Strengthening Churches
